hero.title: Teaching teams to build their own machines.
hero.subtitle: We teach teams to build their own CNC, so they're never stuck waiting on someone else's shop.

heroImage.caption: Hapa Bots X-Carve setup session with GEarheads

impact.label: Why it matters
impact.text: Most rookie teams hit the same wall: they can design a part in CAD, but can't make it. Building your own MPCNC fixes that — and teaches you how machines actually work.

concept.label: The MPCNC Concept
concept.heading: Open-source, low-cost, self-built
concept.subtext: What the MPCNC is, where it came from, and why it works.

inlinePhoto.caption: MPCNC frame mid-build — conduit rails and printed corner blocks before squaring

body: The MPCNC — Mostly Printed CNC — is an open-source router built from 3D-printed parts, conduit, and stepper motors, for well under $500.
Ryan Zellars started it at V1 Engineering; a decade of public development means solid docs and forgiving tolerances. It cuts FTC parts well — brackets, plates, panels.
We walk teams through sourcing hardware, printing parts, squaring the frame, and wiring it up. By the end, they're cutting their own toolpaths and don't need us.

whyItWorks.label: Our Approach
whyItWorks.heading: Why teach teams to build their own machines
body: The usual fix is borrowing parts from a team that has a CNC. Generous, but fragile — it just shifts the dependency.
Building your own changes that. A team that assembles the frame and runs its first cut knows why every bolt matters — no manual teaches that.
Rookie teams gain the most: a first-year team with its own CNC is already ahead of programs years older.
It scales too — the hardware's available anywhere, and our North Carolina pilot proved the knowledge transfers remotely just as well.

teams.name: RedCat Robotics
teams.tagline: First in our region to build and operate their own MPCNC.
teams.description: RedCat was the first local team to finish the full build with no prior machining experience. Their machine now cuts polycarbonate and aluminum, with toolpaths from their own Onshape exports.
highlights: Built the full MPCNC from printed parts to first cut
Moved from borrowing fabrication to in-house production
Generates toolpaths from their own Onshape exports

teams.name: C-Gull Robotics
teams.tagline: A more experienced team that pushed further into toolpaths and materials.
teams.description: C-Gull came in with more experience, so the basics clicked fast. The real work was dialing in feeds and speeds for polycarbonate, HDPE, and aluminum — leaving a repeatable process their students documented.
highlights: Optimized feeds-and-speeds across polycarbonate, HDPE, and aluminum
Developed repeatable toolpath strategies for FTC part geometries
Built student-owned process documentation for future seasons

teams.name: North Carolina Pilot Team
teams.tagline: Proving the program can travel — same approach, different region, same results.
teams.description: A North Carolina team tested whether this only works in person. With us available just for remote troubleshooting, they handled assembly and first cuts alone — and their questions sharpened our documentation for everyone since.
highlights: First out-of-state pilot — tested fully remote delivery
Completed the build with remote-only GEarheads support
Proved the program scales beyond our local ecosystem

teams.name: Hapa Bots
teams.tagline: A different machine, same philosophy — Hapa Bots brought an X-Carve and pushed it further.
teams.description: Hapa Bots already had an X-Carve, so they skipped the build. Getting it competition-ready took nearly as much work — squaring the gantry, tuning stepper current, rebuilding the toolpath workflow. A hobby tool became a real fabrication machine.
highlights: Brought an X-Carve up to spec for aluminum and polycarbonate
Full mechanical re-baseline: squareness, z-axis flex, stepper tuning
Bridged commercial machine ownership into competitive fabrication
